311.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
311.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana warns that wealth gained by harmful deeds does not last and leaves its owner bound by his own passions and hatred.
311.tie_back: Valluvar's stainless people refuse to cause pain even for wealth that would bring them distinction. The Jain verse explains why: wealth gained by evil deeds is lost, and the hatred behind it remains.
311.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
311._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a reasonable thematic fit; the Jain verse argues from consequences, whereas the Kural presents non-harm as a fixed principle (kol).

312.quote_or_event: “A monk should not be angry if beaten, nor should he therefore entertain sinful thoughts; knowing patience to be the highest good, a monk should meditate on the Law. If somebody strikes a restrained, resigned Śramaṇa somewhere, he should think: ‘I have not lost my life.’”
312.explanation: Corporal punishment (vadha) is one of the hardships a Jain monk must bear. When struck, he answers with patience and not even a thought of retaliation.
312.tie_back: Valluvar says the stainless will not hurt in return even someone who has spitefully harmed them. Mahāvīra gives the same rule and extends it to the thought of revenge.
312.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.26–27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
312._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a close match for non-retaliation against deliberate injury, though it is framed as a rule for monks.

313.quote_or_event: “When he who is free from desires approached the village, the inhabitants met him on the outside, and attacked him, saying, ‘Get away from here.’ He was struck with a stick, the fist, a lance, hit with a fruit, a clod, a potsherd. … abandoning the care of his body, the Venerable One humbled himself and bore pain, free from desire.”
313.explanation: During his wanderings in the wild Lāḍha country, Mahāvīra, who had done the villagers no wrong, was beaten, cut and set upon by dogs. He bore it without striking back, 'ceasing to use the stick against living beings.'
313.tie_back: Valluvar warns against retaliating even against people who hate you without any provocation. Mahāvīra's conduct in Lāḍha is the Jain model of exactly that restraint toward unprovoked enemies.
313.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I, Lecture 8 ('The Pillow of Righteousness'), Lesson 3, vv. 7–12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org numbering)
313._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The non-retaliation is exact, but the text does not state the Kural's point that retaliation brings inescapable grief. Some editions number this lecture as the ninth.

314.quote_or_event: “Knowing that he was near, the Blessed One said, ‘Caṇḍakauśika, wake up! wake up! Do not be confused.’ When he heard the Lord’s words, the recollection of his former births arose in the serpent … Then, after he had circumambulated the Lord of Three Worlds three times, free from passions, he undertook a fast of his own accord.”
314.explanation: The poison-eyed serpent Caṇḍakauśika burns and bites Mahāvīra repeatedly. Mahāvīra answers with compassion and a word of awakening, and the serpent, transformed, gives up violence entirely; Mahāvīra stays on 'from compassion for him.'
314.tie_back: Valluvar says the way to punish a wrongdoer is to do him good until he is ashamed, and then let it go. Mahāvīra meets venom with kindness, and that kindness, not a counter-blow, is what turns the serpent away from violence.
314.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. 3, part 10, 'Episode of Caṇḍakauśika' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)
314._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a strong narrative parallel for overcoming harm with goodness. The text speaks of awakening and recollection rather than 'shame', and the same episode is used for Kural 307 (a different part of the story).

315.quote_or_event: “Knowing what is bad, he who knows it with regard to himself, knows it with regard to (the world) outside; and he who knows it with regard to (the world) outside, knows it with regard to himself: this reciprocity (between himself and) others (one should mind).”
315.explanation: At the close of its first lecture on the 'weapon' that harms living beings, the Ācārāṅga makes true knowledge depend on recognising that what hurts oneself hurts others too.
315.tie_back: Valluvar asks what use knowledge is if it does not treat another's pain as one's own. The Ācārāṅga makes the same equation: real knowledge of suffering runs both ways between self and other.
315.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.1.7.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)
315._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a strong fit, since both texts make empathy the test of knowledge, although the Ācārāṅga's immediate context is harm to wind-bodies.

316.quote_or_event: “As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to kill. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to tyrannise over. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to torment. … The righteous man who lives up to these sentiments, does therefore neither kill nor cause others to kill (living beings).”
316.explanation: Mahāvīra grounds non-violence in direct identification with the victim: whatever you would feel is what the other feels.
316.tie_back: Valluvar's negative Golden Rule says never to do to another what you have learned to be painful. The Ācārāṅga's 'as it would be unto thee' rests on the same experiential ground.
316.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.5.5.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)
316._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a near one-to-one match, one of the oldest Indian statements of the reciprocity principle.

317.quote_or_event: “(E. g. big creatures) have one form of bodily existence and then another. But all are subject to pain; hence they should not be killed. This is the quintessence of wisdom: not to kill anything. Know this to be the legitimate conclusion from the principle of the reciprocity with regard to non-killing.”
317.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga calls non-harm toward every being the very core of wisdom, a verse it repeats at I.11.10.
317.tie_back: Valluvar calls not harming anyone, in any degree, at any time, even in thought, the highest virtue. The Jain verse likewise sets universal non-harm at the summit, as the 'quintessence' of wisdom.
317.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.1.4.9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
317._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a strong fit for the Kural's 'anyone, anytime' and its ranking of non-harm as supreme. This verse does not mention harm done in thought, although Jain doctrine elsewhere (bhāva-hiṃsā) clearly includes it.

318.quote_or_event: “All beings are fond of life, like pleasure, hate pain, shun destruction, like life, long to live. To all life is dear.”
318.explanation: The Ācārāṅga states the universal fact on which ahiṃsā rests: every living being values its own life and recoils from pain.
318.tie_back: Valluvar asks why someone who knows his own pain inflicts it on other lives (mannuyir). The Jain sutra answers from the other side: every one of those lives feels what he feels.
318.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.2.3.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)
318._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a near-direct match, and both texts extend the circle of concern beyond humans to all living beings.

319.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
319.explanation: Jacobi's commentator explains the image: a burglar caught halfway through the hole he dug in a wall is crushed when the wall he undermined collapses on him.
319.tie_back: Valluvar says harm done in the morning returns by itself before evening. The burglar is destroyed by his own handiwork almost at once, which shows the same automatic and swift return of one's deeds.
319.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
319._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a strong fit for the self-acting return of harm. Jain karma theory does not ascribe the return to any divine agent, which agrees with the Kural's 'of their own accord' (thaame).

320.quote_or_event: “Whatever cruelty he has done in a former birth, the same will be inflicted on him in the Circle of Births. Having been born in an extremely miserable state of life, the sufferer experiences infinite pain. A wise man hearing of these hells should not kill any living being in the whole world.”
320.explanation: At the end of its description of the hells, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga states that the pain one inflicts is the pain one will suffer, and draws the practical conclusion of non-violence.
320.tie_back: Valluvar says all suffering falls on those who cause it, so those who wish to be free of suffering do not cause it. The Jain verses state both halves, the law and the conclusion, in the same order.
320.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.5.2.23–24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
320._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a close structural match, though it is framed through Jain cosmology of rebirth in hell rather than the Kural's general maxim.
